label: Electric Motor
description: Three-phase induction motor driving pumps, fans, conveyors and similar loads.
general_safety: Isolate and lock out/tag out the motor supply before opening terminal boxes or touching rotating parts.
Let hot surfaces cool, or wear heat-resistant gloves, before touching the casing or bearings.
Only qualified personnel should take electrical measurements on a live motor.
general_inspection: Record the nameplate data (rated current, speed, insulation class) and compare with measured values.
Check visually for dust build-up, loose bolts, burnt smell and damaged cables.
Re-take the readings under steady load for a reliable comparison.

faults.name: Overload
faults.reasoning: Sustained overload raises winding current and heating, so the motor runs hot while vibration can stay normal. A hot motor with low vibration fits this pattern.

triggers.symptom: Casing temperature is high (80 °C or more)
Casing temperature is very high (90 °C or more)
Low vibration points away from a purely mechanical cause
Speed well below a typical 1,450 RPM, possible slip under heavy load
Notes mention overload, tripping or jamming

inspection_steps: Measure running current on all three phases and compare with the nameplate full-load current.
Check the driven load for jamming, a blocked discharge or excess process demand.
Check whether the thermal overload protection is tripping or the starts per hour are too high.
Record temperature against current over a full duty cycle.
maintenance_actions: Reduce the load or correct the process condition causing the extra demand.
Verify overload relay and protection settings against the nameplate.
If the load is genuinely higher than designed, review motor sizing with the responsible engineer.
safety: Do not keep running a motor that trips repeatedly; investigate first.
Use a calibrated clamp meter rated for the voltage when measuring current.

faults.name: Poor ventilation / cooling
faults.reasoning: Dust-clogged cooling fins, a damaged fan or a blocked airflow path stops the motor shedding heat, so it heats up even at normal load. High temperature with low vibration is consistent with this.

triggers.symptom: Casing temperature is high (80 °C or more)
Casing temperature is very high (90 °C or more)
Low vibration points away from a purely mechanical cause
Notes mention dust, a blocked vent or a cooling problem

inspection_steps: Inspect the cooling fan, fan cover and cooling fins for dust, oil film or blockage.
Check clearance around the motor and the ambient temperature of the room or enclosure.
Confirm the fan is intact, turning the right way and firmly fixed.
Compare the temperature after cleaning to see whether it drops.
maintenance_actions: Clean fins, fan and air inlets and remove obstructions around the motor.
Replace a cracked or loose cooling fan.
Improve airflow or add ventilation if the enclosure runs hot.
safety: Lock out the motor before removing the fan cover.
Wear a dust mask and eye protection when cleaning.

faults.name: Bearing friction / lubrication problem
faults.reasoning: Worn, dry or over-greased bearings create friction heat at the shaft ends, usually with growing noise and vibration. Heat alone is weak evidence; noise and vibration make this more likely.

triggers.symptom: High temperature, which bearing friction can cause
Notes mention bearings, grease or grinding

inspection_steps: Measure bearing housing temperature at both ends with an infrared thermometer; a large difference points to one bearing.
Listen with a stethoscope or screwdriver for grinding or rumbling.
Measure vibration at the bearing housings if a meter is available.
Check the greasing history and the grease type used.
maintenance_actions: Re-grease with the specified grease and quantity; avoid over-greasing.
Replace the bearing if it is noisy, discoloured or still runs hot after re-greasing.
Check shaft fit and alignment while the bearing is out.
safety: Lock out the motor before touching the shaft or coupling guard.
Keep the stethoscope or screwdriver clear of exposed rotating parts.

faults.name: Winding insulation degradation
faults.reasoning: Overheating, moisture or ageing degrades winding insulation, which causes more heating and can lead to short circuits. Very high temperature is a warning sign but not proof on its own.

triggers.symptom: Notes mention a burning smell, tripping or insulation problems

inspection_steps: Measure insulation resistance with a megger (motor isolated and discharged) and compare with the acceptable minimum.
Compare winding resistance between the three phases.
Look for discolouration, burnt smell or varnish deterioration at the terminal box.
Check for moisture ingress.
maintenance_actions: Dry out the windings if moisture is found, then re-test.
Plan rewinding or replacement if insulation resistance is low or falling.
Fix the cause of overheating so the repaired insulation is not damaged again.
safety: Insulation testing must be done only on a de-energised, locked-out and discharged motor.
Treat a burning smell or smoke as an emergency: stop the motor and isolate it.

faults.name: Supply voltage problem (low voltage, imbalance or lost phase)
faults.reasoning: Low voltage, voltage imbalance or loss of a phase makes the motor draw extra current and run hotter, with humming, reduced torque and sometimes more vibration.

triggers.symptom: Notes mention voltage, phase or supply problems

inspection_steps: Measure the voltage at the motor terminals on all three phases and calculate the imbalance.
Check fuses, contactor contacts and connections for a lost or loose phase.
Compare phase currents; a large imbalance points to a supply problem.
Check the voltage drop along long cable runs.
maintenance_actions: Tighten or replace loose or burnt connections and replace damaged fuses or contactors.
Correct the supply voltage or imbalance with the electrical team.
Confirm phase-loss protection is fitted and working.
safety: Take voltage measurements only with a rated meter and PPE, by a qualified electrician.
Lock out before re-terminating any connection.

faults.name: Shaft misalignment / coupling problem
faults.reasoning: Angular or parallel misalignment between motor and load shafts loads the bearings and coupling, giving high vibration (often at once or twice running speed), with heat as it worsens.

triggers.symptom: Raised temperature at bearings or coupling
Notes mention alignment, coupling or shaft problems

inspection_steps: Check coupling alignment with a dial gauge or laser alignment tool.
Check for soft foot (a motor foot not seating flat) and loose foundation bolts.
Inspect the coupling for wear, cracks or overheated rubber elements.
Check for pipe strain or base movement.
maintenance_actions: Re-align the motor and driven machine within the coupling tolerance.
Shim or re-grout the base if it is uneven.
safety: Lock out the motor and secure the load before touching the coupling.
